December, 2025 • Benefits and Wellness Office

Ohio experienced a beautiful fall season this year, with warm weather, abundant sunshine and what seemed like a longer than usual amount of time to enjoy the vibrant, colorful leaves. In December, we encourage you to reflect on meaningful experiences from this past year with gratitude, be present in shared moments with friends and loved ones this holiday season and set personal wellness goals moving forward for 2025.  

Healthier Ways for the Holidays

The holidays may be a challenging time to stay healthy – both physically and mentally. With holiday parties full of decadent food and drinks and busy schedules that may not allow time for our normal routines, we may find it difficult to make healthier decisions. We may find ourselves overindulging, leading to holiday weight gain. The holidays are also a stressful time for many. Overbooked schedules, spending time with difficult family members, dealing with loss, and overspending on holiday gifts may all lead to increased stress. With a little forethought and planning ahead, however, it is possible to embrace and enjoy the holiday season.

Read more

Healthier Travel

Pack smart. A travel health kit is a good idea to bring with you when you travel. The CDC recommends filling your travel health kit with over-the-counter medicines and your prescriptions (enough to last your whole trip, plus a little extra), a first aid kit, insect repellent, sunscreen (SPF15 or higher), aloe for sunburns, alcohol-based hand sanitizer, water disinfection tablets, an extra pair of contact lenses or glasses if needed, a thermometer, and your health insurance card.

Learn more

Self-care Invest in Yourself 

The National Institute of Mental Health defines self-care as taking the time to do things that help you live well and improve both your physical and mental health. These acts can help you manage stress, lower your risk of illness, and increase your energy.
Learn more

Financial Well-being

Stress about money and finances may have a significant impact on Americans’ lives. Nearly 72% of adults report feeling stressed about money at least some of the time and nearly 25% say they experience extreme stress about money. The American Psychological Association (APA) recognizes financial stress as the leading cause of unhealthy behaviors like smoking, weight gain, and alcohol and drug abuse. Other behaviors linked to financial stress are gambling and overextending credit balances. Each time an individual turns to these temporary stress relievers, the APA concludes that the stress returns and often at even greater intensity.

Read more

item.title: 2026 Combined PPO & HDHP Open Enrollment: What is an HSA Account?
item.description:
November 11, 2025 | Employee Benefits and Wellness

What is an HSA Account?

A Healthcare Savings Account (HSA) is a tax-advantaged savings account that is paired with a high-deductible health plan (HDHP) that allows you to set aside pre-tax money to pay for qualified medical expenses like deductibles, copayments, and prescriptions. The funds in an HSA roll over year-to-year and stay with you even if you change jobs or retire. Your money can grow interest, and even the interest is tax-free. The money is federal tax-free if it’s spent on a qualified medical expense.

The HSA is owned by the employee and can be funded through employee payroll contributions and through employer contributions. Employer contributions are made in January and July as outlined in your Collective Bargaining Agreement or Ordinance.  

The IRS determines how much you can fund annually. There is no limit on how much money can accumulate, the IRS only limits how much can be deposited each year. Employees can contribute up to the annual maximum amount as determined by the IRS. Maximum contribution amounts for 2026 are:

  • $4,400 for single coverage
  • $8,750 for family coverage

Those 55 years of age or older, but not yet entitled to Medicare benefits, can fund an additional $1,000 per year “catch-up” contribution. If your spouse is 55 or older, they can open an HSA bank account and deposit a $1,000 “catch-up” contribution in addition to these amounts.

You are eligible to open and contribute to an HSA if:

  • You are covered by an eligible high deductible health plan (HDHP) – which means you can’t take the Traditional PPO plan and open an HSA account
  • You are not covered by any other traditional health plan that is not a high deductible health plan (vision & dental is permissible)
  • You are not entitled to Medicare, TRICARE or TRICARE for Life
  • You have not received VA benefits within the past three months unless the care was for a service-related disability
  • You are not claimed as a dependent on someone else’s tax return
  • You are not covered by a Health Care Flexible Savings Account (FSA)

Please see irs.gov/publications/p502 for more information on eligibility and eligible expenses.

item.description:
November 3, 2025 | Employee Benefits and Wellness

How to Decide What Plan Is Right For Me

Selecting a health plan that’s right for you and your family is a big decision that can feel overwhelming.

Experts say that a lack of understanding of your options may result in less-than-ideal selections, which may cause you to miss out on the plan option that might better suit your needs and offer potential cost savings.

This year’s open enrollment is a good chance to review how you and your family is using health services and decide whether you’ll stick with the plan you’ve got or switch. It’s also an opportunity to assess your overall care costs to help ensure you choose a plan that will work best for you and your family's budget.

Below are some things to consider when comparing plan options:

1. Cost

When picking a health insurance plan, you must consider both predictable and variable costs related to your plan to determine your total estimated healthcare expenses for the year. Before you enroll in a plan, research the cost-related aspects of your plan options. This can help you determine which plan serves your budget and needs. Here are some cost-related factors to consider as you're making your decision:

  • What is the Plan Structure for Services(Copays, Coinsurance etc.)
  • Monthly Premiums
  • Plan Deductible
  • Plan Out-of-Pocket Maximum
  • Eligibility for Associated Accounts like HSA with your plan

2. Consider Your and Your Family’s Healthcare Needs

From year to year, your coverage needs may change. Maybe you have different medication needs or a procedure planned for the upcoming year. Before you enroll in a plan, think about the care you or your family may need in the year ahead. Here are some factors to consider as you're making your decision:

  • Medical needs
  • Current Health
  • Services/Specialist
  • Prescription Drug Utilization and Cost
  • Planned Expenses such as Upcoming Procedures

3. Ask Yourself Questions

Below are some questions to ask yourself, when deciding between your plan options. 

  • How much can I afford to pay in monthly premiums?
  • Can I afford/am I comfortable paying a higher deductible if I or a covered dependent needs unplanned medical care?
  • Are my current providers in-network?
  • Can I afford to go out-of-network if my provider is not in network? Am I willing to change to an in-network provider?
  • How often do I expect / expect my covered dependents to need medical care?
  • Do I or my dependents see a specialist or have prescription drugs that are taken regularly? 
  • Do I or a dependent have any planned medical procedures coming up?

4. Review Plan Information and Utilize Plan Resources

  • Plan Information on the Employee Benefits Website
    • Summary Plan Descriptions(SPD)
    • Summary of Benefits and Coverages (SBCs)
    • Prescription Drug List/Formulary
    • Current plan rates
  • Provider look-up tools through carrier portal
  • Attend Open Enrollment Information Session or listen to a playback of a recorded session

October, 2025 • Benefits and Wellness Office

Navigating the Candy: A Dietitian’s Approach to Intuitive Eating During the Holidays

Halloween is around the corner, kickstarting the holiday season along with all of it’s tasty treats. Many of us start to think of these with excitement, others with uncertainty. Do you indulge, abstain, try to find a middle ground, promise to work-out more, or something in between? In this article, explore these challenging question with registered dietitian, Maddie Bidwell, RD, LD, a self-proclaimed holiday foodie whose goal it is to eat good food and feel good while doing it.

Question: Is it possible to enjoy the Halloween candy that I’m surrounded with while also honoring my health goals and if so, what’s the strategy to do this?

Answer: I love to think of Halloween as a time where we can observe where we’re at in our relationship with food. A great illustration of this is when a child goes trick-or-treating and gets to indulge in all their candy that night. Often, instead of practicing moderation, we see them eat as much as they can and then quickly realize the consequences as the stomachache sets in. As adults, often, we may still feel stuck in this cycle. So how do we escape it and feel empowered in our food choices? Whether we have wins or losses this year,  we can learn that our body signals when we’ve had enough and that we can both feel good and enjoy a treat when we practice moderation and be intentional about our food. What does this look like? Let’s consider how we thoughtfully approach this:

  1. Consider objectively what you value and how you’re wired. Ask yourself questions like: “In a perfect world, how would I approach food and wellbeing? Do I thrive in an all or nothing environment? Do I want to honor cravings or not? Am I a quality or quantity eater by nature?” These questions will shape your strategy this season.
  2. Create a plan. Now, that you’ve considered your why and wiring, you can create a strategy. Some folks do well with guidelines for themselves, “I can have one or two pieces of candy each day and enjoy all my favorites in smaller doses.” Others want one day to enjoy more on one day of the week and the rest of the week abstain. Come back often to what’s your why and how you’re wired. When we take the time to consider what matters most to us and then create a plan that honors that, we don’t have to feel guilty when our plan doesn’t look like someone else’s and we can know we’ve thoughtfully and practically planned for our wellbeing both mentally and physically.

What’s your why → Create a plan → Reassess as needed

Question: How do I practice eating mindfully as a beginner, especially if I’ve struggled with this in the past?

Answer: The adult brain is often resistant to change. We settle into our patterns and strengthen preexisting neural pathways. Anytime we want to change, we need to start small, create little victories, and overtime, strengthen new thought pathways. As we head into this holiday season, I encourage you to choose one mindfulness practice and create an achievable plan to implement it. For example, you could make sure to eat a snack before the holiday buffet so that you aren’t starving and feel out of control. You might also choose to use a smaller plate to be more mindful about hunger and fullness cues between servings. Maybe, you’re reminding yourself to do these with alarms on your phone, having an accountability partner, or anchoring these new practices into reoccurring habits of your day. As you think about what you’d like to try, remember, “what’s your why and how are you wired?” These questions will help you find a strategy that works for you.

Below, I’ll walk you through a mindful eating practice that you can use to avoid autopilot at your next holiday feast.

Try this mindful eating technique practice as you prepare for your holiday season:

  1. Use the hunger rating scale: Before you build your plate, take a deep breath and consider on a scale from 1-10 how hungry you are, 1 being absolutely starved and 10 being uncomfortably full. Let this be the deciding factor on how much to fill your plate.
  2. Check in with your environment: Prior to taking a bite, consider how you feel. Is your mouth watering? How does your food smell? Is your stomach rumbling? Is there one thing on your plate that feels the most appetizing? Take a moment to be present with your food and your body to avoid going on auto pilot
  3. Savor each bite: When you take each bite, slow down, intentionally chewing fully, feeling the process of chewing and swallowing, imagining that you’re following that food all the way from your mouth to your stomach.
  4. Mindful Pauses: Between each bite, put down your fork and focus on the chewing experience, taking time for a drink to wash everything down between bites.
  5. Reassess Midway: Halfway through your meal, reconsider how full you are using the hunger rating scale. If you are fully satisfied, stop eating. Remember, you can always come back for more later. If you’re still hungry, continue eating and checking in to notice when you reach the point of being comfortably satisfied.
  6. 15 Minute Break: After you finish a plate of food, give yourself 15 minutes to relax, allow your satiety (satisfaction) cues to kick in and consider how you feel before going back for seconds.

Crock Pot White Chicken Chili

Adapted from: White Chicken Chili [Slow Cooker, Instant Pot + Stovetop]

Servings: 6

Ingredients:

  • 1 rotisserie chicken, deboned & shredded
  • 2 T olive oil
  • 1 white onion, diced
  • 1 can cannelini beans
  • 2 green bell pepper, diced
  • 1 jalapeno, diced
  • 6 cloves garlic, minced
  • 2-3 t ground cumin
  • 2-3 t dried oregano
  • 1 T chili powder
  • 1 t salt
  • 1 t black pepper
  • 2 cups bone broth or chicken broth
  • 1 can full-fat coconut milk
  • Juice of ½ lime
  • 2 T fresh cilantro
  • Optional: 1 t cayenne pepper

Note: Served best with salad & bread

Directions:

  1. In the crock pot, add onions, olive oil, peppers, garlic, beans, chicken, spices & cilantro; combine thoroughly
  2. Add broth and coconut milk, stirring to combine, may choose to add additional seasoning here
  3. Set the crock pot to low for 3-4 hrs (may need to finish on high for 30-60 min)

OCTOBER 2025 – WOMEN’S HEALTH & NATIONAL BREAST CANCER AWARENESS

Women's Health

As our bodies change through the years, so do our health needs and goals. Maybe you’re looking to prevent or plan pregnancy, learn more about menopause or focus on your overall health and well-being. Dive into topics unique to women’s health to help guide and empower your wellness journey at any age or stage of life.

Learn more

Breast Cancer Symptoms and Treatment

Did you know our bodies are constantly growing and replacing cells? The cell growth cycle works on autopilot to produce healthy cells, but sometimes certain genes can mutate. If that happens, cells may grow out of control and form a tumor. Those tumors can either be noncancerous or cancerous. If a cancerous tumor grows in breast tissue, it’s called breast cancer. While statistics suggest that 1 in 8 women will be diagnosed with breast cancer, the rates of diagnosis and death continue to decrease. Better screening, early detection and increased awareness have all played their part to help bring those numbers down. Thinking about the possibility of getting breast cancer may be concerning, but the more knowledge you have, the better chances you may have for catching potential cancers early and making informed decisions about your health.

Read more

Breast Cancer Screening and Diagnosis

When you see a pink ribbon, do you automatically think of breast cancer? Many organizations have done a great job raising awareness for the most common type of cancer among women. In fact, maybe you know at least one person who has been diagnosed. It can be scary stuff. So, it’s important to know the ways we can check our bodies and stay on top of our health. The phrase “better safe than sorry” may ring true when it comes to taking a preventive approach to finding cancer. The key to early detection and diagnosis is knowing which breast cancer tests and screenings are available, and which one may be best for you. You can think of breast cancer tests in two ways: preventive (before or without any symptoms) and diagnostic (after a sign or symptom occurs).

September, 2025 • Benefits and Wellness Office

Top Nutrition Tips to Healthy Aging From a Registered Dietitian:

September is Healthy Aging Month!

Aging is a natural part of life and for folks 45 years and older, this month is designed to celebrate that journey, focusing on helping you become the best version of yourself! One of the ways we can optimize this season of life is through our nutrition.

Check out the following top tips from a dietitian to feel your best and optimize your wellbeing!

Tip 1: Re-energize with whole foods!

One common change with aging is feeling less energized, but we can combat that through how we fuel our body. While it might be tempting to drink more caffeine, both excess caffeine and alcohol have both been shown to cause further fatigue.

Ultra-processed foods high in sugar and low in nutrients can cause your blood sugar levels to dip and spike throughout the day, leaving you feeling drained. Replacing these types of foods with whole food sources will provide you with more nutrients per calorie. Added fiber and protein will help keep blood sugar levels more stable for sustained energy over the course of the day. To learn more, check out this Johns Hopkins article on specific nutrients that may impact your energy levels.

Tip 2: Try on the Mediterranean Diet

Ikaria, Greece, is an area of the world called a blue zone. This culture is marked by a large percentage of centenarians, or folks who live to be at least 100 years old.

One of the factors that’s been researched for this group is the Mediterranean Diet. While, this isn’t the only factor leading to healthy aging, it plays a key role in maintaining physical and mental wellbeing.

The Mediterranean Diet is not a restrictive diet, rather, it focuses on incorporating certain foods in greater quantities and limiting others to achieve an anti-inflammatory diet that reduces risk of developing chronic disease and provides maximal amounts of necessary nutrients like omega-3 fatty acids. While the Mediterranean Diet limits things like added sugar and alcohol; below, are the key components that you can add little by little to make your diet align with this health preventative eating style:

Daily:

  • 3 servings of fruits and vegetables each
  • 3-6 servings of whole grains/starchy veggies
  • 3 servings of dairy
  • 1-4 Tbsp olive oil

Weekly:

  • 3 servings of beans
  • 3 servings of fish
  • 3 servings of nuts

Free Nutrition Counseling

Meet with Maddie for a FREE one on one personalized nutrition counseling session.


Topics often discussed include weight management, disease management or prevention, generalized healthy eating, and more!
Learn more

Sardinian Minestrone

Servings: 10

Ingredients:

  • 7 Tbsp olive oil
  • 1 white onion, chopped
  • 2 carrots, peeled & chopped
  • 2 celery stalks, chopped
  • 2 t minced garlic
  • 1, 28oz can crushed tomatoes
  • 3 yellow potatoes, peeled & diced
  • 1.5 c chopped fennel bulbs & stalks (leeks or celery are a good replacement)
  • 1/4 c parsley, chopped
  • 2 T basil, chopped
  • 1, 15oz can fava beans or cannellini beans
  • 1, 15oz can cranberry beans or pinto beans
  • 1, 15 oz can chickpeas
  • 6-8 cups water
  • 2/3 cup lentils or Israeli couscous
  • 1/2 t salt
  • 1/2 t ground pepper

Directions:

1. Heat 3 tbsp olive oil in a large soup pot or Dutch oven over medium high heat
2. Add onions, carrots, and celery; cook stirring often about 5 minutes. Add garlic and cook till fragrant, about 20 seconds
3. Stir in tomatoes, potatoes, fennel, parsley, basil, drained beans, and chickpeas. Add enough water until everything is submerged by 1 in.
4. Raise the heat to a boil, then reduce to low and simmer uncovered about 10 minutes. Stir in lentils, salt, and pepper, add more water if soup is dry. Simmer until lentils are cooked
5. Pour 1 tbsp olive oil into each bowl before serving

Fiber: 31 g
Total sugar: 10 g
Protein: 31 g
